questions.prompt: What is the primary defense against cross-site scripting (XSS)?

options.text: Context-aware output encoding/escaping of untrusted data

questions.explanation: Encoding untrusted data for its output context makes it render as text, not execute; a Content Security Policy and HttpOnly cookies add depth.

questions.prompt: Match each XSS type to its description.

pairs.right: Malicious script saved on the server and served to viewers
Script from the request echoed straight back into the page
Client-side JS writes untrusted data into the page

questions.explanation: Stored XSS persists on the server, reflected XSS comes from the request, and DOM-based XSS occurs in client-side JavaScript handling of untrusted data.

questions.prompt: What root cause makes CSRF possible?

options.text: Browsers automatically attach a site's cookies to requests, even cross-site

questions.explanation: Because the browser auto-sends cookies (including the session cookie) to a site, a malicious page can cause an authenticated state-changing request.

questions.prompt: Setting a session cookie's ____ attribute to Lax or Strict stops it being sent on cross-site requests, blocking most CSRF.
questions.explanation: SameSite=Lax/Strict tells the browser not to send the cookie on cross-site requests, so forged requests arrive unauthenticated.

questions.prompt: Which are effective CSRF or cookie-hardening defenses? Select all that apply.

options.text: Using GET requests to change state

questions.explanation: Anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite, and HttpOnly/Secure flags harden sessions; using GET for state changes makes forgery easier, not harder.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of a stored-XSS attack.

items.text: Attacker submits content containing a script
The script runs in the victim's session

questions.explanation: Stored XSS: the attacker submits a script, the server saves it without encoding, a victim loads the page, and the script executes in their session.
